title: Road pavement
summary: The flexible versus rigid distinction is the organising idea: a flexible pavement distributes load grain to grain and so needs a strong subgrade (designed on CBR), while a rigid slab bridges on its own flexural strength (designed on the modulus of subgrade reaction k). The fourth power law is the single most consequential result in the subchapter, because it means axle load control matters more than any design refinement. For rigid pavements, keep warping stress (a temperature GRADIENT) apart from frictional stress (a UNIFORM temperature change), since they are relieved by different joints.

sections.heading: Flexible and rigid pavements
sections.body:
**The fundamental distinction, and everything else follows from it:**

| | **FLEXIBLE pavement** | **RIGID pavement** |
|---|---|---|
| **Load distribution** | **GRAIN TO GRAIN**, spreading through successive layers over a widening area | By the **FLEXURAL STRENGTH of the slab**, which **bridges** local weakness |
| **Load spread** | A **narrow cone**, so the subgrade receives a concentrated pressure | A **wide area**, so the subgrade pressure is low |
| **Design parameter** | **CBR** (subgrade **shear strength**) | **Modulus of subgrade reaction k** (subgrade **stiffness**) |
| Subgrade requirement | **Strong subgrade essential** | Can bridge a **weaker** subgrade |
| Deflection under load | **Elastic, recoverable** deflection | Very little deflection |
| **Design life** | **15 years** typically | **30 years** typically |
| Initial cost | **Lower** | Higher |
| Maintenance | **Higher, but easier and incremental** | Lower, but repairs are difficult |
| Riding quality | Good, deteriorates gradually | Excellent, with joint bumps |
| **Stage construction** | **Possible** — layers can be added later | Not practicable |
| Temperature effects | Softens in heat, stiffens in cold | **Warping and expansion stresses** |
| Suitability | The general choice; **stage construction** where funds are limited | **Heavy traffic, urban intersections, industrial areas, waterlogged sites** |

**The load-spread difference is the physical root of the design parameter difference**, and it is worth stating explicitly. A flexible pavement's load reaches the subgrade **concentrated**, so the subgrade must be able to **resist that pressure without shearing** — hence CBR, a strength measure. A rigid slab spreads the load so widely that the subgrade pressure is small; what matters instead is how much the subgrade **deflects** under it, since the slab's stresses depend on the support it receives — hence **k**, a stiffness measure.

**Layers of a flexible pavement**, from the bottom up:

| Layer | Function |
|---|---|
| **Subgrade** | The **prepared natural soil** — the foundation; compacted to ≥ 97% modified Proctor |
| **Sub-base (GSB — granular sub-base)** | Spreads load; **DRAINAGE**; prevents subgrade intrusion into the base |
| **Base course (WBM, WMM or crushed stone)** | The **main structural layer**; distributes the load |
| **Binder course (DBM)** | Intermediate bituminous layer; adds structural strength |
| **Wearing (surface) course (BC)** | **Resists abrasion and weather**; provides **skid resistance** and waterproofing |

**Each layer is stronger than the one below it**, which is the logical structure: the stress is greatest at the top, where the wheel bears, and diminishes with depth as the load spreads — so the material quality can diminish correspondingly. Placing an expensive material low in the pavement wastes it; placing a weak material high fails.

**The granular sub-base's drainage function** is easily overlooked and genuinely important: it provides a **path for water to escape laterally** from the pavement structure, and it prevents the fine subgrade soil being **pumped up** into the base course voids under repeated loading. A pavement with no drainage layer traps water at the subgrade level, where it softens the soil and destroys the support.

**Layers of a rigid pavement:**

| Layer | Function |
|---|---|
| **Subgrade** | Foundation |
| **Sub-base (DLC — dry lean concrete, or GSB)** | Uniform support; prevents **pumping**; a construction platform |
| **Separation membrane** | Prevents bond and moisture movement between slab and sub-base |
| **Concrete slab (PQC — pavement quality concrete)** | The **structural and wearing** layer, both at once |

**Note that in a rigid pavement the slab is both the structure and the surface** — which is why its concrete must satisfy both flexural strength and abrasion requirements, and why a rigid pavement cannot be resurfaced without addressing the slab.

**Semi-rigid and composite pavements** exist between the two: a **cement-treated base** under a bituminous surface behaves partly as each, and a **bituminous overlay on a concrete slab (whitetopping in reverse)** is a composite. They combine advantages but also inherit the joint-reflection cracking problem.

sections.heading: Traffic loading and the fourth power law
sections.body:
**Design traffic** is expressed in **MSA — million standard axles**:

> A **STANDARD AXLE is 80 kN (8160 kg)** — a single axle with dual wheels

**Cumulative standard axles over the design life:**

> **N = 365 × A × [(1 + r)^n − 1]/r × F × D**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **A** | Initial number of commercial vehicles per day (laden weight ≥ 3 tonnes) |
| **r** | Annual **growth rate** (minimum 5% per IRC 37) |
| **n** | **Design life** in years |
| **F** | **Vehicle damage factor (VDF)** — standard axles per commercial vehicle |
| **D** | **Lane distribution factor** |

**The vehicle damage factor and the FOURTH POWER LAW** — the most consequential result in the subchapter:

> **Damage ∝ (axle load / standard axle load)⁴**

**The consequences are dramatic:**

| Axle load | Damage relative to a standard axle |
|---|---|
| 40 kN (half) | (0.5)⁴ = **0.0625** — one sixteenth |
| **80 kN (standard)** | **1.00** |
| 100 kN | (1.25)⁴ = **2.44** |
| **128 kN (60% overload)** | **(1.6)⁴ = 6.55** |
| 160 kN (double) | (2)⁴ = **16** |

**So a 60% overload does about six and a half times the damage, and a doubly loaded axle sixteen times.**

**The practical conclusion is the point:**

> **AXLE LOAD CONTROL matters more than any refinement of pavement design.**

A handful of grossly overloaded trucks can consume more of a pavement's design life than the entire remaining traffic. Conversely, a pavement designed for 10 MSA and then subjected to routine 50% overloading will fail in a small fraction of its intended life — and no amount of additional thickness within a reasonable budget will compensate. That is why **weighbridges and enforcement are pavement engineering measures**, not merely regulatory ones.

It also explains why **passenger cars are effectively irrelevant** to pavement design: a car's axle load of perhaps 10 kN does (0.125)⁴ ≈ **0.0002** of a standard axle's damage. A pavement is designed for **commercial vehicles alone**, and cars are counted only for capacity.

**Typical VDF values (IRC 37)** vary with terrain and the initial traffic volume:

| Terrain / traffic | VDF |
|---|---|
| **Hilly, low traffic** | **0.5** |
| Plain, up to 150 CVPD | 1.5 |
| **Plain, over 1500 CVPD** | **4.5** |

The higher VDF at higher volumes reflects the fact that busier routes carry a greater proportion of heavy, fully laden vehicles.

**Lane distribution factor D**:

| Carriageway | D |
|---|---|
| Single lane | 1.0 |
| Two-lane single carriageway | **0.75** of total in both directions |
| Four-lane divided | 0.40 |

**Design life:**

| Road | Design life |
|---|---|
| **National highway, expressway** | **15 years** |
| Other roads | 10 – 15 years |
| **Rigid pavement** | **30 years** |

The rigid pavement's longer design life reflects both its greater durability and the impracticality of strengthening it later — a flexible pavement can receive an overlay, a concrete slab essentially cannot.

sections.heading: Flexible pavement design
sections.body:
**The evolution of methods** is worth knowing because questions reference the older ones:

| Method | Basis |
|---|---|
| **Group Index method** | An empirical index from the soil's grading and plasticity; **superseded** |
| **CBR method (older IRC 37)** | Design curves of thickness against CBR and traffic |
| **Triaxial, McLeod, Burmister** | Various empirical and layered-elastic approaches |
| **IRC 37:2018 — MECHANISTIC-EMPIRICAL** | **Current** — computes stresses and strains, then checks them against performance criteria |

**The mechanistic-empirical method of IRC 37:2018** checks **two failure criteria**, and both must be satisfied:

| Criterion | Strain checked | Failure mode |
|---|---|---|
| **FATIGUE** | **Horizontal TENSILE strain at the BOTTOM of the bituminous layer** | **Fatigue cracking**, appearing as **alligator (crocodile) cracking** at the surface |
| **RUTTING** | **Vertical COMPRESSIVE strain at the TOP of the SUBGRADE** | **Rutting** — permanent deformation in the wheel paths |

**Why those two locations** is the instructive part. The bituminous layer acts as a **beam in bending** over the more flexible layers below, so its **underside is in tension** — and bituminous material is weak in tension and fails by fatigue under repeated flexure. The **subgrade** is the weakest layer and receives the load in **compression**, so it accumulates permanent deformation there. Between them, the two criteria capture the pavement's two distinct ways of failing.

**So the design process is:**

1. Determine the **design traffic in MSA** and the **subgrade CBR**.
2. **Assume a layer composition** (thicknesses and moduli).
3. Compute the **critical strains** using layered elastic analysis (IITPAVE software, or the IRC catalogues).
4. Check both against the **allowable strains** for the design traffic.
5. **Revise and repeat** until both are satisfied.

IRC 37 provides **design catalogues** — tabulated pavement compositions for combinations of traffic and subgrade CBR — which is how the method is applied in ordinary practice without running the analysis.

**Subgrade preparation requirements:**

| Requirement | Value |
|---|---|
| **Compaction** | ≥ **97%** of modified Proctor MDD (**100%** for the top 500 mm on a major road) |
| **Design CBR** | Soaked, 4 days; commonly the 90th percentile of results |
| **Minimum CBR** | Subgrade CBR below about **2%** requires **improvement or replacement** |
| **Water table** | Kept **0.6 – 1.0 m** below the formation level |
| Expansive soil | Removed, replaced, or stabilised with lime |

**Drainage is a structural requirement, not a refinement.** Water in a flexible pavement:

| Effect | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Softens the subgrade** | Reduces CBR, so the pavement is effectively under-designed |
| **Strips the binder** from the aggregate | Loss of cohesion, ravelling, potholes |
| **Pumps fines** upward under repeated loading | Contaminates the granular layers |
| **Freezes** (at altitude) | Frost heave and thaw weakening |

So the drainage provisions — **camber, side drains, a drainage layer, subsurface drains where the water table is high, and cross drainage** — are as much part of the pavement design as the layer thicknesses. **A well-designed pavement with poor drainage fails; a modest pavement with good drainage survives.** That is the single most useful practical judgement in the subchapter.

**Overlay design.** An existing pavement is strengthened by an overlay, and the required thickness is determined from its **structural condition**, measured by the **Benkelman beam**:

> The **rebound deflection** under a standard axle is measured at intervals; the **characteristic deflection** is computed, corrected for **temperature, seasonal variation and subgrade moisture**, and the overlay thickness read from **IRC 81** curves against the design traffic.

**Higher deflection means a weaker pavement, hence a thicker overlay** — and the corrections matter because deflection varies substantially with temperature (bitumen softens) and season (subgrade moisture), so an uncorrected measurement can mislead by a large factor. Modern practice uses the **Falling Weight Deflectometer (FWD)**, which measures the whole deflection basin and allows the moduli of individual layers to be back-calculated.

sections.heading: Rigid pavement design and construction
sections.body:
**Three stress systems act in a concrete pavement slab**, and keeping them apart is the most examined point in the subchapter:

| Stress | Cause | Relieved by |
|---|---|---|
| **LOAD stress** | **Wheel load** — analysed at the **interior, edge and corner** | Slab **thickness** |
| **WARPING (temperature) stress** | A **temperature GRADIENT through the slab DEPTH** | **WARPING joints** (longitudinal, along the centreline) |
| **FRICTIONAL stress** | A **UNIFORM temperature change**, resisted by **subgrade friction** | **EXPANSION and CONTRACTION joints** |

**Warping and frictional stresses are the pair most often confused**, and the distinction is precise:

> **WARPING** arises from a temperature **GRADIENT** (top hotter or cooler than bottom) which makes the slab try to **CURL**; the self-weight and adjacent slabs restrain it.
> **FRICTIONAL** arises from a **UNIFORM** temperature change which makes the whole slab try to **expand or contract**; the friction of the subgrade restrains it.

Different causes, different restraints, **different joints**.

**Warping behaviour through the day:**

| Time | Gradient | The slab tries to |
|---|---|---|
| **DAY** | Top **hotter** | **Curl DOWNWARD at the edges** (convex up) |
| **NIGHT** | Top **cooler** | **Curl UPWARD at the edges** (concave up) |

The stresses are largest where the gradient is steepest — **around midday** and **just before dawn**. **Bradbury's coefficients** give the warping stress from the gradient, the slab dimensions and the radius of relative stiffness.

**Westergaard's load stress analysis** gives the stress at three critical positions:

| Position | Character |
|---|---|
| **Interior** | Load well away from any edge; the slab is supported all round |
| **Edge** | Load at a free edge; support on one side only |
| **Corner** | Load at a corner; **least support** — often the most critical |

**The radius of relative stiffness** is the parameter on which the analysis rests:

> **l = [E h³ / (12 k (1 − μ²))]^{1/4}**

It measures **how far the slab spreads a load** — a stiffer or thicker slab on a softer subgrade spreads it further.

**The critical design combination:**

> **Critical stress = LOAD stress + WARPING stress**, evaluated at the **edge and corner**

because those are the weakest positions and because the warping and load stresses there are **additive** in the critical season. Frictional stress is considered separately, in fixing the **joint spacing**.

**Joints — each relieving its own stress:**

| Joint | Relieves | Spacing | Detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| **EXPANSION joint** | **Expansion** in hot weather | **50 – 140 m** | Full-depth gap with a filler board, sealed; **dowel bars** across |
| **CONTRACTION joint** | **Shrinkage and contraction** | **≈ 4.5 m** (plain slab) | A **groove cut or formed to about ¼ depth**, inducing a crack below it; **dowel bars** |
| **WARPING (longitudinal) joint** | **Curling** stresses | Along the **centreline**, at lane widths | **Tie bars** across |
| Construction joint | End of a day's work | As required | — |

**The contraction joint's mechanism is worth understanding:** it does not prevent cracking — it **controls where the crack forms**. A groove cut to a quarter of the depth creates a **plane of weakness**, so the inevitable shrinkage crack forms **beneath the groove**, in a straight line, where it can be sealed. Without the groove the slab cracks randomly.

**Dowel bars and tie bars are NOT the same thing**, and the distinction is examinable:

| | **DOWEL bar** | **TIE bar** |
|---|---|---|
| Located at | **Expansion and contraction (transverse)** joints | **Longitudinal (warping)** joints |
| Function | **Transfers LOAD** across the joint | **Holds the two slabs TOGETHER** |
| Bonded? | **Plain, greased, sliding** at one end — it must **permit movement** | **Deformed, fully bonded** — it must **resist separation** |
| Design for | **Load transfer** (bending, bearing, shear) | **Tension** (the frictional force of the adjacent slab) |

So a **dowel permits movement while transferring load**; a **tie bar prevents movement**. Reversing them defeats both purposes — a bonded bar across an expansion joint prevents the expansion it exists to allow.

**Design procedure (IRC 58)** for a jointed plain concrete pavement:

1. Determine the **design traffic** (commercial vehicles, axle load spectrum) and the **effective k** on top of the sub-base.
2. Select a **trial slab thickness**.
3. Compute the **flexural stress** at the critical locations for the axle load spectrum, in **day and night** temperature conditions.
4. Compute the **cumulative fatigue damage** and check it does not exceed 1.
5. Check **corner stress**, and the **bottom-up and top-down cracking** cases.
6. Revise and repeat.

**Concrete requirements:** **flexural strength** is the design property (**minimum 4.5 N/mm² at 28 days** for PQC), not compressive strength — because the slab fails in **bending**. Compressive strength is specified as a control measure (typically **M40**), and the relation **f_cr = 0.7√f_ck** links them.

**Construction methods:** **fixed form paving** (side forms, screed or vibrating beam) for small works, and **slip form paving** for major projects — a machine that extrudes the slab continuously without side forms, giving higher output and better uniformity.

**Texturing** the fresh surface (by brushing, tining or grooving) provides **skid resistance** — a concrete surface is otherwise dangerously smooth when wet. **Transverse tining** is usual; **longitudinal** grooving is quieter.

**Curing is critical for a concrete pavement** because of its very large **surface-to-volume ratio**: it loses moisture faster than any other concrete element, and it is exposed to sun and wind immediately. **Curing compounds or wet coverings for at least 14 days** are specified, and inadequate curing produces **plastic shrinkage cracking within hours** and a weak, dusting surface thereafter.

**Continuously reinforced concrete pavement (CRCP)** and **prestressed** pavements avoid transverse joints altogether, accepting fine cracks held tight by continuous reinforcement — eliminating the joint bumps and the maintenance that joints require, at higher initial cost.

**Roller compacted concrete (RCC)** is a very dry mix placed and compacted like a bituminous layer with a roller; cheap and quick, used for industrial pavements and dam construction.

**Which pavement to choose:**

| Choose RIGID where | Choose FLEXIBLE where |
|---|---|
| **Very heavy traffic** and long design life | Moderate traffic |
| **Urban intersections and bus bays** (standing and turning loads) | Open highway |
| **Waterlogged or weak subgrade** that cannot be improved | Good subgrade available |
| Industrial areas, ports, container yards | — |
| Good aggregate and cement available; bitumen expensive | Bitumen and aggregate available |
| **Long-term economy** is the criterion | **Low initial cost** or **stage construction** is needed |

**Stage construction is the flexible pavement's decisive advantage in Nepal**: a road can be built as a gravel or thin bituminous surface within the available budget and **strengthened later by overlay** as traffic grows and funds allow. A concrete pavement must be built to its full thickness at once, which is often not affordable — so flexible pavements dominate, and the choice reflects finance as much as engineering.

formulas.label: Flexible versus rigid — design parameter
formulas.expression: FLEXIBLE: grain-to-grain load transfer → design on CBR (shear strength). RIGID: slab flexure → design on k (stiffness).
formulas.note: The load reaches the subgrade concentrated in a flexible pavement and spread in a rigid one.

formulas.label: Cumulative standard axles
formulas.note: Standard axle 80 kN. F is the VDF, D the lane distribution factor. Growth rate minimum 5%.

formulas.label: The FOURTH POWER law
formulas.note: A 60% overload does 6.5× the damage; double load 16×. Axle load control matters more than design refinement.

formulas.label: IRC 37:2018 failure criteria
formulas.expression: FATIGUE: tensile strain at the BOTTOM of the bituminous layer. RUTTING: compressive strain at the TOP of the subgrade.
formulas.note: The bituminous layer bends, so its underside is in tension; the subgrade is compressed and deforms permanently.

formulas.label: Radius of relative stiffness
formulas.note: Measures how far the slab spreads a load. The basis of Westergaard's and Bradbury's analyses.

formulas.label: Rigid pavement stress systems
formulas.expression: LOAD (wheel) + WARPING (temperature GRADIENT) + FRICTIONAL (UNIFORM temperature change)
formulas.note: Critical combination = load + warping, at edge and corner. Warping → warping joints; frictional → expansion/contraction joints.

formulas.label: Joint spacing
formulas.expression: expansion 50–140 m ; contraction ≈ 4.5 m ; warping along the centreline
formulas.note: A contraction joint does not prevent cracking — it controls WHERE the crack forms.

formulas.label: Dowel bars and tie bars
formulas.expression: DOWEL: transverse joints, plain and greased, TRANSFERS LOAD while permitting movement. TIE: longitudinal joints, deformed and bonded, HOLDS SLABS TOGETHER.

formulas.label: Concrete for a rigid pavement
formulas.expression: flexural strength ≥ 4.5 N/mm² at 28 days ;   f_cr = 0.7√f_ck
formulas.note: FLEXURAL strength is the design property, because the slab fails in bending.

formulas.label: Overlay design
formulas.expression: Benkelman beam rebound deflection, corrected for temperature, season and subgrade moisture → IRC 81 curves
formulas.note: Higher deflection means a weaker pavement and a thicker overlay. FWD is the modern equivalent.
